title: Overview and justification
body:
This course assumes you already have a revision strategy built around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge, and already know that active techniques outperform passive review. By the end you will be able to select and apply specific techniques from across the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families. You will be able to match your choice of technique to the format of the exam ahead of you. You will also be able to plan and monitor your own performance on exam day itself.

None of this assumes a fixed sequence to follow. It assumes you are ready to design your own combination of techniques and run your own exam-day performance, and shows you what that combination needs to account for.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: select and apply specific active techniques, across visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families, to your own revision material
match your choice of revision technique to the type of exam you are preparing for
plan and monitor your own performance on exam day, from arrival through to writing to time

title: Signpost
body: The course has four short lessons. First, the active-technique toolkit itself: the specific techniques within the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families. Second, matching your choice of technique to the type of exam you are preparing for, not only to the material. Third, performing on exam day itself, from arrival to writing to time. Fourth, bringing the toolkit, the exam-type match and exam-day execution together into one monitored performance. Work through them in order; the last lesson depends on the first three.
instruction: Work through the four lessons in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: By this point you already have a revision strategy, built around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge, and you already know that active techniques outperform passive review. This lesson looks at what that active revision can actually be made of: a toolkit of specific techniques, grouped into visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families, rather than a single method applied regardless of what the gap needs.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not choosing a family here; you already know how to do that. The aim at this stage is to open each family up and see what it actually contains, so that selecting a technique becomes a design decision rather than a default. The same gap in your knowledge can often be closed by several different techniques, and part of the skill is knowing more than one.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: name specific techniques within the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families, for example mind maps, flashcards and mnemonics, reading aloud and discussion, spatial placing and role-play
evaluate, in a worked example, why combining several specific techniques outperforms relying on a single default
design a toolkit of specific techniques, drawn from more than one family, for a module in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body:
The visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families each contain several distinct techniques, not one. Visual techniques include mind maps, visual note-taking, flashcards, mnemonics and posters, each of which forces a different kind of compression and recall. Auditory techniques include reading aloud, recording yourself and explaining material in discussion, each of which tests whether you can produce an explanation rather than only recognise one. Kinaesthetic techniques include spatial placing, role-play, movement and physical models, each of which ties recall to an action rather than a page.

A toolkit is the set of specific techniques you can actually call on, across more than one family, rather than the single technique you happen to reach for first. The point of building one is not variety for its own sake: different techniques expose different kinds of gap, so a toolkit closes more of them than any one technique can on its own.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look at your current revision toolkit. How many specific techniques, across the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families, are actually in it, as opposed to relying on one default? Which family have you never properly tried, and why might that be worth changing?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: The visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families each contain several specific techniques, not one. You can now name techniques within each family, evaluate why combining several outperforms a single default, and design a toolkit drawn from more than one family for your own material. The next lesson turns to matching a technique, once chosen, to the format of the exam it is actually preparing you for.

title: Orientation
body: You now have a toolkit of specific techniques across the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families. This lesson asks a different question: does the technique you have chosen suit not only the material, but the exam you are actually going to sit? A technique that builds the right knowledge can still rehearse the wrong kind of performance if it ignores the exam's format.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: This is a judgement call, not a lookup table. The aim is to get into the habit of checking an exam's format before settling on a technique, so the fit between the two becomes something you design rather than something you discover too late, in the exam itself.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: distinguish how different exam formats, for example essay-based, short-answer and practical, call for different revision techniques
evaluate, in a worked example, why a technique that suits the material can still suit the wrong exam format
match your own revision techniques to the format of an exam in {{context}} you are preparing for

title: Concept: definition
body:
An exam format is the shape the exam itself will take: whether it asks for extended essays, short factual answers, or a practical demonstration, and how much time it gives for each. Matching technique to format means checking that a technique rehearses the kind of performance the format will actually demand, not only that it covers the right material.

A mind map can show you how ideas connect, which supports an essay-based exam well. The same mind map does little to prepare you for a short-answer exam, which rewards fast, precise recall of discrete facts over connected argument. The material can be identical; the format decides which rehearsal actually transfers.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about an exam you are preparing for right now. Does the technique you have chosen suit the format of that exam, or only the material? What would change if you matched the technique to the format instead?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A technique that suits the material can still suit the wrong exam format. You can now distinguish how exam formats call for different techniques, evaluate why format and material can pull in different directions, and match your own technique to the format of an exam ahead of you. The next lesson turns from preparing with the right technique to performing well on exam day itself.

title: Orientation
body: Everything so far has been preparation: building a toolkit of techniques, and matching them to the exam's format. This lesson turns to the exam itself, as something you perform rather than simply sit. Arriving, reading the instructions, allocating time per answer and writing to time are all stages of that performance, and each can be planned for in advance.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: None of this replaces the revision you have already done. It assumes the knowledge is largely in place, and asks a different question: once you are sitting the exam, what turns that knowledge into marks, and what stages of the exam itself need a plan of their own.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify the stages of exam-day performance: arrival, reading the instructions, allocating time per answer and writing to time
evaluate, in a worked example contrasting two students, how planning and monitoring time changes an exam performance
plan your own time allocation for an exam in {{context}} you are about to sit

title: Concept: definition
body:
Exam-day performance has stages, and each one shapes what follows. Arriving early enough to settle, rather than arriving at the last possible moment, affects how clearly you can read what comes next. Reading the instructions properly, including how many questions to answer and from which sections, prevents a plan built on a wrong assumption about what is required.

Allocating time per answer, based on the marks available rather than how comfortable a question feels, sets a budget before you start writing. Writing to that budget, and noticing when you are falling behind it, is what turns a time plan into something that actually holds across the whole paper rather than only the first answer.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think back to your last exam. Which stage of exam-day performance, arrival, reading the instructions, allocating time, or writing to time, cost you the most, and why? What would you monitor differently next time?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Exam-day performance has stages, arrival, reading the instructions, allocating time and writing to time, and each one shapes what follows. You can now identify those stages, evaluate how planning and monitoring time changed one student's performance, and plan your own time allocation for an exam ahead of you. The final lesson brings the toolkit, the format match and this exam-day plan together into one monitored performance.

title: Orientation
body: You now have three separate pieces: a toolkit of specific techniques, a way of matching technique to exam format, and a plan for performing on exam day itself. This lesson connects them. Run on their own, each piece helps. Run together, they become one optimised, self-monitored performance rather than three separate jobs.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: This is not a fourth skill to learn; it is the other three, kept visibly connected rather than handled in isolation. The aim is to be able to trace, for any exam you are preparing for, which technique you are using, which format it is matched to, and how you will monitor your time on the day, as one chain rather than three disconnected decisions.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect a specific technique from the toolkit to the exam type it suits best
connect your exam-day time plan to the format of the exam you are facing
synthesise toolkit, exam-type matching and exam-day self-monitoring into one optimised performance for a module in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body:
An optimised, self-monitored performance is what results when the toolkit, the format match and the exam-day plan inform one another rather than being decided separately. The toolkit tells you what techniques are available. The format match tells you which of those techniques actually rehearses this exam. The exam-day plan tells you how that preparation will be spent once you are in the room.

Self-monitoring is what keeps the chain live rather than fixed in advance. A technique chosen weeks ago, matched to a format you checked at the time, still needs checking against how the exam is actually going on the day, so that a slipping time plan can be corrected before it costs you the rest of the paper.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Pick a module you are revising for right now. Can you trace, in one sentence each, which specific technique you will use, which exam format it is matched to, and how you will monitor your time on the day? Where is that chain weakest?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A toolkit of techniques, a match to the exam's format and a monitored exam-day plan work best as one connected chain, not three separate jobs. You can now connect a technique to the exam type it suits, connect your time plan to the exam's format, and synthesise all three into one optimised, self-monitored performance of your own. That is the performance this course has been building toward.

displayTitle: Why might relying on a single default revision technique undersell what the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families together offer?
body: Why might relying on a single default revision technique undersell what the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families together offer?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why might relying on a single default revision technique undersell what the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families together offer?

_items.text: Because different techniques expose different kinds of gap, so one default can leave some gaps undetected.
_items.feedback: Yes. A single technique tests your knowledge in only one way, however well it suits some material.

_items.text: Because a default technique always takes longer to apply than switching between several.
_items.feedback: Speed is not the reason a single default falls short here.

_items.text: Because exam boards penalise candidates who are known to use only one revision technique.
_items.feedback: Exam boards have no visibility of, or interest in, your revision technique.

_items.text: Because the three families were designed to be used in strict rotation.
_items.feedback: The families are not a fixed rotation; the point is choosing what fits, not cycling through all three.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A single default technique only tests knowledge in one way, whatever else it has going for it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a default technique can and cannot reveal about a gap.

displayTitle: What does building a toolkit of specific techniques let you do that knowing the three families alone does not?
body: What does building a toolkit of specific techniques let you do that knowing the three families alone does not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does building a toolkit of specific techniques let you do that knowing the three families alone does not?

_items.text: Choose a technique that fits the specific material in front of you, not just its general family.
_items.feedback: Yes. A family name alone does not tell you which specific technique within it fits a given topic.

_items.text: Avoid needing to test yourself on any topic more than once.
_items.feedback: A toolkit does not remove the need for repeated testing on difficult material.

_items.text: Guarantee that revision takes less time overall.
_items.feedback: A wider toolkit is not primarily about reducing time; it is about fit.

_items.text: Remove the need to know which family a technique belongs to.
_items.feedback: Knowing the family is still useful; the toolkit adds specific options within it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Specific techniques let you match the technique to the material, not just the family.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a family name can tell you, and what it cannot.

displayTitle: Why can a technique that suits your material still be the wrong choice for a given exam format?
body: Why can a technique that suits your material still be the wrong choice for a given exam format?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why can a technique that suits your material still be the wrong choice for a given exam format?

_items.text: Because the exam format determines what kind of recall or performance you actually need to practise.
_items.feedback: Yes. A technique can build the right knowledge while still rehearsing the wrong kind of performance for the exam ahead.

_items.text: Because exam formats change every year, making any fixed technique useless.
_items.feedback: Exam formats within a module are typically stable; this is not about yearly change.

_items.text: Because a technique that suits the material always takes too long to apply.
_items.feedback: Time is not the issue being described here.

_items.text: Because material-matched techniques cannot be combined with any other technique.
_items.feedback: Techniques can be combined; the issue is format fit, not combinability.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The exam format shapes what kind of performance you need to rehearse, not only what knowledge you need.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the exam format itself asks you to do, beyond knowing the material.

displayTitle: What should you check about an exam, beyond the material it covers, before settling on a revision technique?
body: What should you check about an exam, beyond the material it covers, before settling on a revision technique?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you check about an exam, beyond the material it covers, before settling on a revision technique?

_items.text: The format the exam will test you in, for example essay-based, short-answer or practical.
_items.feedback: Yes. The format determines what kind of practice the technique needs to provide.

_items.text: The exact room the exam will be held in.
_items.feedback: The room itself does not change which technique fits the exam.

_items.text: The number of other students sitting the same exam.
_items.feedback: The number of other candidates has no bearing on technique choice.

_items.text: The colour of the exam paper.
_items.feedback: This has no bearing on which technique fits the exam.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The exam's format is what tells you which kind of technique will actually prepare you for it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what changes depending on how the exam will actually test you.

displayTitle: Why does writing to time depend on decisions made earlier in an exam, such as reading the instructions and allocating time per answer?
body: Why does writing to time depend on decisions made earlier in an exam, such as reading the instructions and allocating time per answer?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does writing to time depend on decisions made earlier in an exam, such as reading the instructions and allocating time per answer?

_items.text: Because a time plan made without reading the instructions properly can be built on a wrong idea of what is required.
_items.feedback: Yes. Writing to a plan only helps if the plan itself was built on an accurate reading of the exam's requirements.

_items.text: Because writing speed is fixed and cannot be affected by planning.
_items.feedback: Writing speed is not the issue; the plan behind the writing is.

_items.text: Because exam instructions are usually irrelevant to how time should be spent.
_items.feedback: Instructions are often exactly what tells you how time should be allocated.

_items.text: Because allocating time per answer only matters if you finish early.
_items.feedback: Time allocation matters throughout the exam, not only if time is left over.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A time plan is only as good as the reading of the exam's own requirements that it was built on.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a time plan is actually based on.

displayTitle: What is lost if you plan your exam-day time in advance but do not monitor it once the exam has started?
body: What is lost if you plan your exam-day time in advance but do not monitor it once the exam has started?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is lost if you plan your exam-day time in advance but do not monitor it once the exam has started?

_items.text: The ability to notice and correct a plan that is already slipping before it costs you an entire answer.
_items.feedback: Yes. A plan made in advance still needs checking against the clock while the exam is actually running.

_items.text: Nothing; a plan made in advance works regardless of what happens during the exam.
_items.feedback: A plan made in advance can still go wrong once the exam is under way, which is why monitoring matters.

_items.text: The chance to read the instructions, since that only happens once planning is finished.
_items.feedback: Reading the instructions happens before planning, not as a result of monitoring.

_items.text: The requirement to allocate time to each answer in the first place.
_items.feedback: Allocating time happens during planning; monitoring is what checks the plan is being kept to.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Monitoring is what lets you catch a slipping plan in time to correct it, rather than only noticing at the end.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what planning alone cannot do once the exam is actually running.

title: Explore the concept
body: Open each family below to see the specific techniques inside it.
instruction: Select a heading to open it.

_items.title: Visual
_items.body: Mind maps, visual note-taking, flashcards, mnemonics and posters. Each compresses material differently: a mind map shows structure, a flashcard isolates a single fact, a mnemonic encodes a sequence.

_items.title: Auditory
_items.body: Reading aloud, recording yourself and explaining material in discussion. Each tests whether you can produce an explanation out loud, not only recognise one on a page.

_items.title: Kinaesthetic
_items.body: Spatial placing, role-play, movement and physical models. Each ties recall to a physical action, so the technique itself rehearses retrieval rather than only exposure.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students are preparing the same module, and both know that active revision beats passive review.

{{learner-a}} has settled on flashcards as a default, and applies them to every topic on the outline. Flashcards work well for isolated facts and definitions, but several of this module's topics are long, branching processes. Pressed into flashcard form, each process becomes a flat list of steps, and {{learner-a}} can recite the list without being able to explain why one step leads to the next.

{{learner-b}} starts from the same outline but sorts topics by what kind of knowledge each one actually is. Definitions and isolated facts still go onto flashcards. The branching processes go onto a mind map, so the structure between steps is visible, not just the steps themselves. One especially difficult process, which {{learner-b}} has struggled to retain by sight alone, gets talked through out loud and recorded, then played back during a commute.

Both students use active techniques. Only {{learner-b}}'s toolkit is wide enough to match the kind of knowledge each topic actually demands.

title: Building your own toolkit
body: Use these questions to start building a toolkit of specific techniques for a module in {{context}}, rather than defaulting to the one you reach for first.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Have I sorted my topics by the kind of knowledge each one actually is, rather than treating them all the same?
Have I matched at least one specific technique, not just a family, to each kind of topic?
Have I tried a technique outside the family I default to, for at least one topic?
Have I kept more than one technique in reserve for a topic that resists the first one I try?
Could I name, for my hardest topic, which specific technique I am using and why?

displayTitle: Formative check: what a toolkit adds beyond knowing the three families
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: what a toolkit adds beyond knowing the three families

_items.text: The ability to choose a specific technique that fits the kind of knowledge a topic actually is.
_items.feedback: Yes. Knowing a family is not the same as knowing which technique inside it fits a given topic.

_items.text: A guarantee that every topic takes the same amount of time to revise.
_items.feedback: A toolkit does not equalise time; different topics still take different amounts.

_items.text: The ability to avoid testing yourself on topics you find comfortable.
_items.feedback: A toolkit is about fit, not about which topics you choose to avoid testing.

_items.text: Permission to use only one family of technique for the whole module.
_items.feedback: A toolkit is built precisely because one family rarely fits every topic.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A toolkit lets you match the technique to the kind of knowledge, not just name its family.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a family name can tell you, and what it leaves you still having to decide.
_incorrect.final: A toolkit's value is matching a specific technique to what a topic actually is, which a family name alone cannot do.

displayTitle: Formative check: what the second student's sorting changed
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: what the second student's sorting changed

_items.text: Match each topic to the specific technique suited to the kind of knowledge it actually involves.
_items.feedback: Yes. Sorting by knowledge type let the technique fit the topic, not just the family.

_items.text: Finish revising the module faster than the first student.
_items.feedback: Speed of revision is not what the worked example compares.

_items.text: Avoid using flashcards anywhere in the plan.
_items.feedback: Flashcards still appear in the second student's plan, for the topics they actually suit.

_items.text: Guarantee that every process topic would be fully memorised.
_items.feedback: Sorting improves fit; it does not guarantee complete memorisation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Sorting topics by what kind of knowledge they are let the technique match the topic.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what sorting by knowledge type specifically let the second student do.
_incorrect.final: The sorting let the second student match technique to the kind of knowledge each topic actually was, not simply apply one default throughout.

displayTitle: Formative check: applying the toolkit idea
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: applying the toolkit idea

_items.text: Work out what kind of knowledge each topic is, then choose a specific technique to fit it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Starting from the kind of knowledge, not the family, is what this lesson has set out.

_items.text: Pick the family you find quickest to apply and use it throughout.
_items.feedback: Speed of application is not the basis for choosing a technique here.

_items.text: Use flashcards for every topic, since they are the most widely applicable technique.
_items.feedback: No single technique, including flashcards, suits every kind of topic equally well.

_items.text: Choose a technique at random for each topic, to avoid bias toward a favourite.
_items.feedback: Randomness removes the deliberate matching this lesson has been building toward.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Working out what kind of knowledge a topic is, then matching a specific technique to it in {{context}}, is the move this lesson has described.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what should come first: the family you prefer, or the kind of knowledge the topic actually is.
_incorrect.final: The strongest approach works out what kind of knowledge the topic is first, then matches a specific technique to it in {{context}}.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students are preparing for exams on closely related material, each confident in the technique they have chosen.

{{learner-a}} builds a detailed mind map connecting every concept in the module, and revises almost entirely from it. The exam, when it arrives, is a short-answer paper: forty discrete questions, each wanting one precise fact in a few seconds. {{learner-a}} knows how the concepts connect, but struggles to pull a single fact out of the map quickly enough, and runs out of time with answers half-written.

{{learner-b}} starts by checking the exam's own past papers before choosing a technique, and finds the same short-answer format. Flashcards become the main technique, one fact per card, drilled for speed rather than connection. A short mind map is still made, but only as a one-off orientation exercise, not the main revision method.

Both students know the material. Only {{learner-b}}'s technique was chosen to match what the exam would actually ask them to do.

title: Matching technique to format
body: Use these questions to check a chosen technique against the format of an exam in {{context}}, before you commit your revision time to it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Have I checked the exam's actual format, for example past papers or a specification, rather than assuming it?
Does my chosen technique rehearse the kind of performance this format will demand, for example speed, connection or procedure?
Have I timed myself using this technique under conditions similar to the exam itself?
If the material suits one technique but the format suits another, have I decided which should take priority?
Could I explain, in one sentence, why this technique fits this particular exam's format?

displayTitle: Formative check: why format matters alongside material
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: why format matters alongside material

_items.text: Because a technique can rehearse the right knowledge while still practising the wrong kind of performance for the exam.
_items.feedback: Yes. Knowing the material is not the same as rehearsing the performance the format will actually demand.

_items.text: Because exam formats are decided at random each year and cannot be anticipated.
_items.feedback: Exam formats within a module are generally stable and can be checked in advance.

_items.text: Because material-matched techniques always take longer to revise with.
_items.feedback: Time is not the reason format matters here.

_items.text: Because format only matters for practical exams, not written ones.
_items.feedback: Format matters across essay-based, short-answer and practical exams alike.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A technique that fits the material can still rehearse the wrong kind of performance for the exam's format.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what knowing the material does and does not guarantee about the exam itself.
_incorrect.final: Format matters because it determines what kind of performance, beyond knowledge alone, the exam will actually test.

displayTitle: Formative check: what checking the format first changed
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: what checking the format first changed

_items.text: Choose a technique that rehearsed fast, precise recall, matching the short-answer format ahead.
_items.feedback: Yes. Checking the format told the second student which kind of rehearsal would actually transfer.

_items.text: Learn the material in less depth than the first student.
_items.feedback: Depth of learning is not what the worked example compares.

_items.text: Avoid making a mind map at all.
_items.feedback: A mind map still appears in the second student's preparation, used differently.

_items.text: Guarantee a higher mark than the first student.
_items.feedback: Matching technique to format improves fit; it does not guarantee a specific mark.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Checking the format first told the second student which kind of rehearsal would actually transfer on the day.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what checking the format specifically let the second student decide.
_incorrect.final: Checking the format let the second student choose a technique rehearsing the right kind of performance for it, rather than the material alone.

instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.

_items.text: Check the exam's format, then choose a technique that rehearses the kind of performance it demands.
_items.feedback: Yes. Starting from the format, not the material alone, is the move this lesson has described.

_items.text: Choose whichever technique you enjoy most, since enjoyment improves retention regardless of format.
_items.feedback: Enjoyment does not substitute for checking the format's actual demands.

_items.text: Assume the format will resemble last year's exam without checking.
_items.feedback: Assuming without checking risks missing a change in format.

_items.text: Pick the technique that covers the material fastest, regardless of format.
_items.feedback: Speed of coverage does not guarantee the technique fits the exam's format.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Checking the format of an exam in {{context}} first, then matching a technique to it, is the strongest approach.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which should come first: the technique you prefer, or the format the exam will actually take.
_incorrect.final: The strongest approach checks the exam's format in {{context}} first, then chooses a technique that rehearses what that format demands.

title: Explore the concept
body: Open each stage below to see what it involves.
instruction: Select a heading to open it.

_items.title: Arrival
_items.body: Arriving with time to settle, rather than at the last possible moment, affects how clearly you can read what follows.

_items.title: Reading the instructions
_items.body: Checking how many questions to answer, from which sections, and how marks are distributed, before you write a word.

_items.title: Allocating time per answer
_items.body: Setting a time budget per answer based on the marks available, not on how comfortable the question feels.

_items.title: Writing to time
_items.body: Noticing when you are falling behind your own budget, and moving on, rather than overrunning one answer at the expense of the rest.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students sit the same exam, equally well revised.

{{learner-a}} arrives just as the doors close, skims the instructions quickly and starts writing on the first question that looks familiar. Caught up in that answer, {{learner-a}} loses track of time and is still writing it when half the exam's time has passed, leaving the remaining questions to be rushed in what is left.

{{learner-b}} arrives early enough to sit quietly before the exam starts, reads the instructions fully, including the mark distribution across sections, and writes a rough time budget per answer in the margin before starting. When one answer runs over its budget, {{learner-b}} notices, stops, and moves to the next question, returning to finish the first answer only if time allows at the end.

Both students know the material equally well. Only {{learner-b}}'s performance on the day was planned and monitored rather than left to run on its own.

title: Planning your exam-day performance
body: Use these questions to plan your performance for an exam in {{context}}, before the day itself arrives.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Have I planned to arrive with enough time to settle, rather than at the last possible moment?
Do I know how many questions to answer, from which sections, and how marks are distributed?
Have I worked out a time budget per answer, based on marks available rather than comfort?
Have I decided what I will do if an answer is running over its budget?
Could I explain, in one sentence, my plan for monitoring time once the exam has started?

displayTitle: Formative check: why exam-day stages need their own plan
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: why exam-day stages need their own plan

_items.text: Because strong revision can still be undone by how time is managed once the exam itself has started.
_items.feedback: Yes. Knowledge in place does not by itself control how time is spent once the exam begins.

_items.text: Because exam instructions are the same for every exam and so do not need reading each time.
_items.feedback: Instructions vary between exams; this is exactly what makes reading them necessary each time.

_items.text: Because arrival time has no effect on how an exam is performed.
_items.feedback: Arrival time affects how settled a candidate is when the exam starts.

_items.text: Because writing speed is fixed and cannot be managed during the exam.
_items.feedback: Writing speed is not fixed in the sense described; time allocation can still be managed.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Revision prepares the knowledge; exam-day stages govern whether that knowledge is used well under time pressure.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what revision does and does not control once the exam itself begins.
_incorrect.final: Exam-day stages need their own plan because strong revision can still be undone by poor time management once the exam has started.

displayTitle: Formative check: what planning and monitoring changed
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: what planning and monitoring changed

_items.text: Notice when an answer was overrunning its time budget and move on before it cost the rest of the paper.
_items.feedback: Yes. Monitoring against a plan let the second student catch and correct the overrun in time.

_items.text: Know the material in more depth than the first student.
_items.feedback: Depth of material knowledge is not what the worked example compares.

_items.text: Avoid reading the exam instructions at all.
_items.feedback: The second student reads the instructions fully; this is part of what changed the outcome.

_items.text: Guarantee that every answer would be finished in full.
_items.feedback: Planning and monitoring improves the chances of covering the paper; it does not guarantee every answer is finished in full.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Monitoring against a time plan let the second student catch a slipping answer before it cost the rest of the paper.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what planning and monitoring specifically let the second student notice and do.
_incorrect.final: Planning and monitoring let the second student notice an overrunning answer and move on in time, protecting the rest of the paper.

instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.

_items.text: Read the instructions fully, set a time budget per answer, and monitor it once writing starts.
_items.feedback: Yes. This sequence is the exam-day plan this lesson has set out.

_items.text: Start writing on the first familiar question immediately, to build momentum.
_items.feedback: Starting without reading the instructions risks missing what the exam actually requires.

_items.text: Allocate equal time to every answer regardless of the marks available.
_items.feedback: Equal time ignores the fact that marks, and therefore expected effort, can differ between answers.

_items.text: Decide on a time budget in advance, then ignore it once writing begins.
_items.feedback: A budget that is not monitored during writing cannot catch an answer that is overrunning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading the instructions, setting a time budget, and monitoring it while writing in {{context}} is the exam-day plan this lesson has described.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which stage this lesson places before the time budget itself, and which comes after.
_incorrect.final: The strongest plan reads the instructions first, sets a time budget per answer, and monitors it while writing in {{context}}.

title: Explore the concept
body: Three cards connecting a technique, its exam format and the exam-day stage it supports.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Technique
_items.subtitle: chosen from the toolkit
_items.text: A specific technique, for example flashcards or a mind map, selected because it suits the kind of knowledge a topic actually is.

_items.title: Format match
_items.subtitle: checked against the exam
_items.text: The same technique checked against the exam's actual format, so it rehearses the kind of performance that exam will demand.

_items.title: Exam-day monitoring
_items.subtitle: kept live on the day
_items.text: The resulting time plan monitored while writing, so a slipping answer is caught and corrected before it costs the rest of the paper.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students prepare for exams across a whole module, both having built a toolkit of techniques and knowing how to match technique to format.

{{learner-a}} treats these as three separate jobs. The toolkit gets built early in the term, format-checking happens once, a few weeks before each exam, and the time plan is drawn up the night before and never looked at again once the exam starts. Each piece is sound on its own, but nothing connects them once the exam is actually under way, and a slipping answer on the day goes uncorrected because no one is watching the clock against the original plan.

{{learner-b}} keeps the three strands visibly connected throughout. The toolkit is reviewed against each exam's format as it approaches, not once at the start of term. The time plan drawn up from that format check is written where it can be checked during the exam itself, and {{learner-b}} glances at it after each answer, adjusting the remaining time if one answer has overrun.

Both students built the same three pieces. Only {{learner-b}} kept them connected and live once the exam itself began.

title: Connecting the three strands
body: Use these questions to check that your toolkit, format match and exam-day plan are connected, rather than three separate jobs, for a module in {{context}}.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Can I name, for my next exam, which specific technique I am using from my toolkit?
Have I checked that technique against this exam's actual format, not an earlier or assumed one?
Have I written a time plan I can actually see and check during the exam itself, not only the night before?
Do I have a plan for what to do if an answer is overrunning its time budget on the day?
Could I trace, in one sentence each, the technique, the format match and the monitoring plan for this exam?

displayTitle: Formative check: what connects the three strands
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: what connects the three strands

_items.text: Each strand informing the others, so the technique, the format match and the exam-day plan are checked against each other rather than fixed separately.
_items.feedback: Yes. Connection comes from each strand being checked against the others, not from doing all three in isolation.

_items.text: Doing all three strands equally thoroughly, regardless of whether they inform one another.
_items.feedback: Thoroughness alone does not create connection if the three strands never check against each other.

_items.text: Completing the toolkit before starting on format-checking, and format-checking before the time plan.
_items.feedback: A fixed order does not by itself keep the strands connected once the exam is under way.

_items.text: Relying on the time plan alone, since it is drawn up last.
_items.feedback: The time plan still needs to reflect the technique and format decisions that came before it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Connection means each strand is checked against the others, kept live rather than fixed once and left.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what keeps the three strands working together, rather than simply existing alongside each other.
_incorrect.final: The three strands are connected when each one is checked against the others, not merely completed separately.

displayTitle: Formative check: what the second student's connection changed
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: what the second student's connection changed

_items.text: Catch and correct a slipping answer during the exam itself, because the time plan was being actively checked.
_items.feedback: Yes. Keeping the plan visible and checked let the second student correct the overrun while the exam was still running.

_items.text: Build a larger toolkit than the first student.
_items.feedback: The size of the toolkit is not what the worked example compares.

_items.text: Avoid checking the exam's format at all.
_items.feedback: The second student checks format as each exam approaches; this is part of what changed the outcome.

_items.text: Guarantee every exam across the module would go equally well.
_items.feedback: Connecting the strands improves the chances of a good performance; it does not guarantee an equal outcome every time.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Keeping the time plan visible and checked let the second student correct a slipping answer while the exam was still running.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what staying connected during the exam itself specifically let the second student notice and do.
_incorrect.final: Staying connected let the second student notice a slipping answer during the exam and correct it, rather than only reviewing afterwards.

displayTitle: Formative check: applying the connected performance
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Formative check: applying the connected performance

_items.text: Check your chosen technique against the exam's format, then keep the resulting time plan visible and monitored during the exam itself.
_items.feedback: Yes. This connected sequence is what this lesson has set out as one optimised performance.

_items.text: Finish building the toolkit, checking the format and writing the time plan as three separate tasks completed well in advance.
_items.feedback: Completing the three tasks separately in advance does not keep them connected once the exam is under way.

_items.text: Rely on the toolkit alone, since it took the most time to build.
_items.feedback: Time invested in the toolkit does not replace checking it against format and monitoring it on the day.

_items.text: Decide on a time plan and avoid checking it again once the exam has started, to stay calm.
_items.feedback: Not checking the plan removes the chance to correct a slipping answer before it costs the rest of the paper.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Checking technique against format, then keeping the time plan visible and monitored during an exam in {{context}}, is the connected performance this lesson has described.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what keeps the three strands working together once the exam in {{context}} has actually started.
_incorrect.final: The strongest approach checks technique against format, then keeps the resulting time plan visible and monitored throughout the exam in {{context}}.
